By Nolan Kido · About this writing

Learn to follow a no-limit Texas hold’em hand and explain your next decision. Poker Foundations is a free first course: start with the cards, then connect betting, position, the board and possible opposing hands through six core lessons.

For complete beginners and players who know the rules but lose track of the action. Use a deck, counters or paper. The lessons and practice are open to everyone, with no signup or purchase.

One small task per visit is enough. Each core lesson begins with one idea, a worked example and a changed situation to explain before revealing the answer. Use that short lesson, then pause or continue. The fuller article is there when you need more detail. The reading estimate covers this whole page, including explanations and the printable card; it is not the length of a class.

The six lessonsFinish the courseChoose extra practiceCard basicsRehearse betting

What you will learn to explain.

  • Which five cards make your hand, and how they compare at showdown.
  • Whose turn it is, which actions are available and how many additional chips a call costs.
  • How position, the changing board and possible opposing hands affect a decision.
  • What a bet is trying to achieve, and which assumptions you still need to check.

Work toward explaining a changed situation with the lesson closed. Opening every page is not a skill test, and this course does not establish readiness to play for money.

Build understanding in six connected stages.

This is one route through standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em: actions and cards, preflop context, the flop, the river, ranges, then betting purpose. Each lesson begins with a limited first pass. Read those sections, explain the check below without the answer, then use a fresh situation to see what needs repair. The longer examples remain available as references.

Use a deck, counters or paper. No wager, playing account or purchase is needed. When the cards themselves are unfamiliar, read card basics and one worked selection, then begin lesson 1. You can pause anywhere or try the checkpoint first when you already know the mechanics.

Start lesson 1: Cards, actions and the pot

Need smaller steps? The beginner practice room pairs six short worked examples with 18 changed questions. Start with one skill; use mixed practice later to choose what to revisit.

Need to practice what happens next at the table? Rehearse one betting round: take each seat’s turn, enter extra counters and follow a line of your own.

  1. Cards, actions and the pot

    Learn: read your two cards, distinguish checking from calling, find the player whose turn it is and compare the best five cards. The lesson finishes with a complete hand whose chips reconcile.

    Before moving on: explain what you owe now, rather than repeating the last number announced. Use only your contribution on this betting round when counting a call.

    Quick check: You posted a big blind of 2 and face a raise to 7. How much more is a call?

    5 more: 7 - 2 = 5. Assume you have enough chips, there is no ante and you made no other preflop contribution. Your posted 2 is already part of this street's wager. Calling brings your preflop total to 7; it does not add a new 7. On a later street, those earlier chips would not pay for a fresh bet.

    If you counted 7 or carried a previous street's payment forward, revisit counting the new chips, then explain the difference again without the answer open.

  2. Your starting hand in context

    Learn: describe position, earlier action, effective stacks and the price before asking whether two cards are worth playing. A hand's label leaves out most of the decision.

    Before moving on: distinguish information you observed from an assumption about hidden cards. Name who still has a turn, including a player who may raise after your call.

    Quick check: At a six-player table, three players fold before you on the button. Are you the last player to act preflop?

    No. The small blind and big blind still have their initial decisions. You have seen three folds, which gives you more information than acting first. It does not reveal either blind's cards or prevent a raise. If you reach a flop against a blind, the button acts after that blind in the initial postflop order. Being later preflop and having position after the flop are related, but not identical.

    If the order was unclear, revisit counting who still has a turn. Draw six seats and move a marker through the action.

  3. Your first decisions after the flop

    Learn: name the made hand and the draw separately, read checks and raises without inventing the opponent's cards, and notice when a helpful shared card improves the other hand too.

    Before moving on: explain both what your cards make now and what they still need. A possibility to improve is different from a completed hand or a guaranteed win.

    Quick check: You hold ace-nine of hearts on a flop of nine of spades, six of hearts and two of hearts. Pair, flush, or draw?

    A pair of nines with an ace kicker, plus a heart-flush draw. Your current best five are 9-9-A-6-2. There are four hearts among your five available cards, so one more heart would complete a flush. You do not already have one. An opponent could have a stronger made hand, and completing your draw does not guarantee that you win.

    If you chose only one label, revisit made hands and draws. Lay out the five cards and count the hearts once each.

  4. The turn, river and showdown

    Learn: rebuild the hand when a new card arrives, recognize that a missed draw can still have showdown value, and distinguish calling a bluff from making one. On the river there is no further community card to rescue a draw.

    Before moving on: separate the price of a call from evidence that your hand meets it. Say when the action is complete and whether you are counting outright wins or a share of the pot.

    Quick check: A heads-up river pot is 30 before a bet of 10. Does a 20% call price prove you should call?

    No. The arithmetic gives the price, not your hand's equity. Assume a fictional cash-game hand, no fees or side pots, enough chips to call and a call that ends betting. The bet makes the current pot 40. Your additional 10 makes 50, so the break-even share is 10 / 50 = 20%. You still need a justified model of the opponent's hands and your expected share, including ties. This does not compare calling with every possible raise.

    If you divided by 40 or treated the price as a measured win chance, revisit the river-call explanation.

  5. Your first range

    Learn: separate known cards, physically possible hands and assumptions about their frequency. You do not need a chart or percentages for the first pass.

    Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown.

    Quick check: You hold A♥ J♥. Can the opponent hold A♥ Q♣? Does a check prove they are weak?

    Neither claim works. The exact A♥ Q♣ is impossible because your ace of hearts cannot be in two hands. Other legal hands remain possible, and a check does not establish their strength or frequency. Revisit known cards and possible hands if either possibility became a fact.

  6. Betting with a purpose

    Learn: name which worse hands might call a value bet or which better hands might fold to a bluff. Compare a bet with checking when nothing is owed.

    Before moving on: describe the response you need, rather than using “I have a pair” or “I won the pot” as the whole argument.

    Quick check: Your bet makes every worse hand fold and every better hand call. Has “I have a pair” justified a value bet?

    No. Under that supplied response pattern, the worse hands do not pay and the better hands are the only callers. You still need to compare the bet with checking and examine the assumptions. This is a hypothetical response pattern, not a claim about actual players. Revisit worse hands that actually call.

Keep your place without another account.

Download the blank beginner study card (TXT), or copy three prompts onto paper: “The lesson I reached,” “What I can explain without looking,” and “One thing to revisit.” Save a lesson's ordinary link with your note. The website does not save your progress, collect your answers or send a reminder.

Each lesson now begins with a short sequence: learn one idea, follow a worked example, then explain a changed situation before opening its answer. Use the next-lesson button when you can explain the difference; the full reference and extra practice are optional. The blank study card includes those changed situations for your own notes.

When a check feels difficult, use its repair link rather than restarting the whole path. When you can explain it, continue to the next stage. After the six stages, try the checkpoint and return later for a fresh explanation. Finishing these exercises is not evidence of a profitable strategy or readiness to risk money. Learning without playing for money remains a complete option.

ONE SCRIPTED HAND
Six players start with 100 counters. Blinds 1/2. No ante, fees or side pots.
You are on the button with ace of hearts and jack of hearts.
The actions are supplied for learning, not betting recommendations.

1. Before the flop: follow the seats
Six players start with 100 counters each. The small blind posts 1 and the big blind posts 2. There is no ante, fee or side pot. Three players fold. You are on the button, the seat marked by the dealer marker. Both blinds still have their first decisions.
After your initial action on the button, who still has an initial decision?

Bring the lessons together, then return later

Finished the six lessons? Follow Hand A across all four betting rounds. Explain before opening the feedback, and reveal the result last. Return later for Hand B: the position, completed draw and call price change.

For a guided example and repeated attempts, use the beginner practice room. After the stage you are studying, try its matching checkpoint situation. After all six, choose a pair of unfamiliar situations and explain them with the lesson closed. The aim is to use an idea in a changed setting, rather than recognize a paragraph you just read.

Try the beginner checkpoint to see which explanation to revisit. It offers six situations, explanations of common mistakes and six changed situations to retry. Choose two, give your own reason first, then use the exact repair link that fits the difficulty. A familiar-looking answer is more useful when you can explain a new example too.

Keep the blank checkpoint workbook (TXT) in your own notes. Record your first reason, one thing you corrected and what happened on the retry. The website does not collect those answers. If wording or navigation still gets in the way, use the optional reader-feedback prompts; they lead to the existing contact form and explain what it asks for.

If you are comfortable with those ideas, you can choose a specific live-play preparation guide or an optional study task below. There is no requirement to start playing for money.

Return later and explain a changed situation

At your next study session, close the lesson and try two checkpoint questions before reopening the explanation. Pick different situations on a later day. A possible routine is a short recall check at the next session and another later in the week; this is a practical suggestion, not a tested optimal schedule for poker.

  1. Recall: say the rule or question in your own words without looking.
  2. Change the example: use the checkpoint’s changed situation, not just the same answer letter.
  3. Repair one gap: follow the precise lesson link, then explain the difference.
  4. Keep one note: record the skill, the mistake and the link to return to. Pause when the task is done.

Use the six-stage study card for your own notes. It includes the route, guided-hand prompts and a later-review plan. Answers and progress are not sent to the website.

Why the course uses examples, explanations and return visits

The Institute of Education Sciences recommends combining worked examples with problem solving, asking for explanations, using retrieval practice and spacing study. Those general findings informed this design. They do not validate this poker course or establish a learning rate for its readers. Read the IES practice guide.

Poker mechanics were checked October 15, 2026 against PokerStars’ Hold’em rules and hand rankings. Their strategy suggestions are not adopted as answers to the scripted hand. External poker publishers may advertise gambling.

If an explanation is still difficult, follow its repair link and try again. If you can explain the changed situation, choose one next task below. There is no certificate or required purchase.

  • Keep practicing: use one mixed set in the beginner practice room, then keep one question to revisit.
  • Prepare for a first game: use the first-session guide to choose a format and check its procedures and full cost. You can keep practicing without a wager.
  • Follow a video: open the poker viewer guide and describe one hand before looking at its result.
  • Study further: choose the cash-game study path or first live tournament preparation when you have a question in that format.

Tell me which explanation was unclear. Include the lesson and the point where you got stuck; keep your private study notes to yourself.

Start with the cards and the goal.

You win a hand when every other player folds, or by having the strongest five-card hand among players who reach the showdown. A tied best hand can share the pot. You do not have to bet on every turn to keep playing; the guided hand below explains the actions.

A standard deck has 52 different cards: thirteen ranks in each of four suits. The usual high-to-low rank order is A K Q J T 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2. A is ace, K king, Q queen, J jack and T ten. The four suits are spades ♠, hearts ♥, diamonds ♦ and clubs ♣. Suits do not outrank one another.

You receive two private cards. The shared board arrives as three cards on the flop, one on the turn, then one on the river. Once all five shared cards are out, choose the strongest five from your seven available cards. Use zero, one or two private cards. An ace can be low in A-2-3-4-5, but a straight cannot wrap through K-A-2-3-4.

What beats what? Open the visual ranking reference

Read strongest to weakest. A royal flush is the highest straight flush. Compare the hand category first, then the relevant ranks and kickers. There is no sixth-card tiebreaker.

  1. Royal flush

    The ace-high straight flush, the highest possible hand.

    A♠K♠Q♠J♠10♠

  2. Straight flush

    Five consecutive ranks in one suit.

    9♥8♥7♥6♥5♥

  3. Four of a kind

    Four equal ranks plus one side card.

    Q♣Q♦Q♥Q♠2♦

  4. Full house

    Three of one rank and two of another.

    J♥J♦J♠4♣4♦

  5. Flush

    Five cards of one suit, not consecutive.

    A♣J♣8♣5♣2♣

  6. Straight

    Five consecutive ranks, not all one suit.

    9♠8♦7♥6♣5♠

  7. Three of a kind

    Three equal ranks and two unmatched side cards.

    8♠8♥8♦K♣3♠

  8. Two pair

    Two different pairs and a side card.

    K♠K♥5♣5♦2♠

  9. One pair

    One pair and three unmatched side cards.

    10♠10♥A♣7♦3♣

  10. High card

    None of the combinations above.

    A♠J♦9♣6♥3♠

    Follow one hand, one decision at a time.

    Use counters or paper. The actions are scripted to explain the rules and accounting; they are not betting recommendations. Read a scene, give your reason, then compare it with the explanation. You can continue after any answer.

    Return to the six-lesson map. No account or wager is needed.

    Six scenes, from the first action to the result.

    1. 1. Before the flop: follow the seats

      Six players start with 100 counters each. The small blind posts 1 and the big blind posts 2. There is no ante, fee or side pot. Three players fold. You are on the button, the seat marked by the dealer marker. Both blinds still have their first decisions.

      1. First seat: folded
      2. Next seat: folded
      3. Cutoff: folded
      4. Button: you
      5. Small blind: posted 1
      6. Big blind: posted 2

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      No shared cards yet.
      Pot now
      3
      Your stack behind
      100
      Big blind behind
      98
      After your initial action on the button, who still has an initial decision?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      The small blind and big blind still act. Before the flop, the initial action begins to the left of the big blind and proceeds clockwise. A raise can give earlier players another decision. The button is last in the initial order after the flop, not before it.

      A. Three folds do not finish the round. Both blinds still have decisions.

      B. Yes. The two seats after the button still have their initial decisions.

      C. The small blind still acts before the big blind. Its forced post was not its initial decision.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    2. 2. Preflop: add only what is missing

      For this scripted practice hand, you raise to 6 total and the small blind folds. The big blind already posted 2 on this betting round and faces your total wager of 6. The current pot is your 6, the folded small blind's 1 and the big blind's 2: 9.

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      No shared cards yet.
      Pot now
      9
      Your stack behind
      94
      Big blind behind
      98
      How many additional counters does the big blind need to call?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      The call adds 6 - 2 = 4. The big blind's total contribution becomes 6. The pot then contains 6 + 1 + 6 = 13, and both remaining players have 94 behind. The folded small blind's counter stays in the pot. This explains the accounting, not whether either action is a good strategy.

      A. Six is the total wager. The big blind has already paid 2 of that total on this round.

      B. Adding the posted 2 to the total 6 counts those forced chips twice.

      C. Yes. Subtract the big blind's 2 already paid from the total wager of 6.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    3. 3. The flop: name what you have now

      The big blind calls. The flop, the first three shared cards, is jack of spades, seven of hearts and two of hearts. The big blind checks, meaning it makes no bet. Your private cards remain ace of hearts and jack of hearts.

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      J♠7♥2♥
      Pot now
      13
      Your stack behind
      94
      Big blind behind
      94
      Which description fits your cards on this flop?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      Your current best five are J-J-A-7-2. You have a pair of jacks with an ace kicker, plus four hearts among your available cards. Another heart could complete a flush, but a possible improvement is not a completed hand or a guaranteed win. After the check you can check or bet; you do not call when nothing is owed.

      A. Yes. The two jacks make a pair; your two hearts plus two on the board make four hearts.

      B. A flush needs five hearts. Only four hearts are available to you now.

      C. The board's jack and your private jack already make a pair, even though you also have a draw.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    4. 4. A flop raise: count this round again

      The scripted line continues: you bet 4 and the big blind raises to 12 total on the flop. The pot is now the previous 13 plus your 4 plus the opponent's 12: 29. Your preflop contribution belongs to an earlier round.

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      J♠7♥2♥
      Pot now
      29
      Your stack behind
      90
      Big blind behind
      82
      How many more counters would a flop call add?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      The call adds 12 - 4 = 8, making the pot 37. Each remaining player has put in 6 preflop and 12 on the flop, leaving 82 from the original 100. You may instead fold or make a legal raise; checking is unavailable against the unmatched wager. The accounting does not establish which choice is best.

      A. Twelve is the opponent's total flop wager. Your 4 on this round already pays part of it.

      B. Yes. Match 12 total after accounting for your 4 already paid on the flop.

      C. The raise is to 12 total, not by another 12 on top of your bet of 4.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    5. 5. The river: rebuild the hand

      You call the extra 8. The turn is nine of clubs; both players check, so nobody pays more on that round. The river is four of diamonds, the last shared card. The big blind bets 10 into the pot of 37, making the current pot 47.

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      J♠7♥2♥9♣4♦
      Pot now
      47
      Your stack behind
      82
      Big blind behind
      72
      Which statement is justified before you decide?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      Your best five are J-J-A-9-7. The flush did not arrive, but your pair remains. A call adds 10 and makes a final pot of 57; a fold or legal raise is also available. There is no universally correct action supplied here because the opponent's hidden hands and their frequencies have not been established.

      A. There are still only four hearts available, and an unmatched river bet prevents checking.

      B. The river is the fifth and final shared card. No later card will complete this missed draw.

      C. Yes. The missed flush leaves your pair, and no earlier-round payment covers this new bet.

      Optional after stage 4: if a call ends this heads-up cash-game hand, 10 / 57 is about 17.54%. With no fees or side pots this prices a call in chips; it does not measure your hand's equity or prove that calling is correct.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    6. 6. Showdown: separate the result and the reason

      For the final scripted action, you call 10. The big blind reveals queen of hearts and jack of diamonds. Compare each player's best five. This is one fictional ending, not evidence about how frequently an actual opponent bluffs or bets for value.

      Your private cards

      A♥J♥

      Shared board

      J♠7♥2♥9♣4♦

      Opponent at showdown

      Q♥J♦
      Pot now
      57
      Your stack behind
      72
      Big blind behind
      72
      Which conclusion follows from this ending?

      Say your answer and the reason, then reveal the explanation.

      Explanation and a repair link

      Your J-J-A-9-7 beats the opponent's J-J-Q-9-7 because the ace kicker outranks the queen. You paid 6 + 12 + 10 = 28 and receive 57, for a net gain of 29. Your stack finishes at 129; the big blind has 72 and the folded small blind has 99. The three earlier folders still have 100 each. All six stacks sum to the original 600 counters.

      A. Yes. Your ace kicker wins, and receiving the pot includes getting back your own contributions.

      B. You receive 57, but 28 of it is your own earlier contribution. The net gain is 29.

      C. One ending does not compare your choices against the alternatives or validate an assumed range.

      Revisit the exact lesson section.

    Rehearse a betting round with counters.

    Know the cards but lose track of the action? Take turns for all three seats. Choose an action and enter the counters to add. The pot, payments and next turn change with your choices. Try one round, then pause or continue to the lessons.

    These are fictional rule exercises with no cards or recommended plays. Imagine every player has enough counters. Stack limits, all-ins, side pots, antes and fees are omitted. Amounts are whole counters, with a practice ceiling of 1,000 per player on this round. That ceiling is not a no-limit poker rule.

    Five actions, in plain language
    Check
    Add nothing when you owe nothing. Keep your hand.
    Bet
    Open wagering on a postflop round. Here the opening bet is at least 2, the big blind.
    Call
    Match the current total wager. Add only the difference from what this seat paid on this round.
    Raise
    Increase the total wager by at least the last full bet or raise. The big blind is a live wager before the flop.
    Fold
    Give up the hand when facing a wager. Earlier payments stay in the pot. Use checking when you owe nothing in this exercise; folding when not facing a wager can violate live tournament procedure.

    A round ends only when every remaining player has had its required turn and answered the latest wager. If only one player remains, the hand ends immediately. A check does not prevent another player from betting later.

    Before the flopA fresh flopFacing a raise

    Before the flop: the big blind still gets a turn

    A three-player table has a button, small blind and big blind, clockwise in that order. Blinds are 1 and 2. The button acts first. Try calling around, then try a different legal line.

    Use counters or paper. Choose an action for the next seat, move only the extra counters, then name who still needs a turn. Compare with the worked line when ready.

    See one worked line for this starting point
    1. Button: call; add 2. The button adds 2, matching the live big blind.
    2. Small blind: call; add 1. The small blind adds only 1 to the 1 already posted. All three have now paid 2, but the big blind has not taken its turn.
    3. Big blind: check. The big blind checks its option. It could instead raise. Now the round ends and the flop can be dealt; the pot is 6.

    This is one legal line. Other legal choices are possible, and none is graded as a good strategy.

    On the flop: a check can be followed by a bet

    The same three seats reached the flop with 6 in the pot. Payments on this new round start at zero. The small blind acts first. Try checking around, then restart and add a bet or raise.

    Use counters or paper. Choose an action for the next seat, move only the extra counters, then name who still needs a turn. Compare with the worked line when ready.

    Starting payments on this betting round

    See one worked line for this starting point
    1. Small blind: check. Checking adds nothing and keeps the small blind in the hand.
    2. Big blind: bet; add 4. The big blind opens betting for 4. This gives the small blind another decision, even though it already checked.
    3. Button: call; add 4. The button adds 4. The small blind still needs to respond.
    4. Small blind: call; add 4. The small blind matches the 4. Everyone remaining has responded to the latest wager; the round ends with 18 in the pot.

    This is one legal line. Other legal choices are possible, and none is graded as a good strategy.

    Facing a raise: count only the new counters

    There was 6 in the pot before this flop round. The small blind bet 4, the big blind raised to 10 total, and the button folded. The small blind acts again. Try a call, then restart to compare a fold or a full raise.

    Use counters or paper. Choose an action for the next seat, move only the extra counters, then name who still needs a turn. Compare with the worked line when ready.

    1. Small blind: call; add 6. The call adds 10 minus 4 = 6, making 26 in the pot. No earlier-street payment reduces this amount. A full raise would need to reach at least 16 total, adding at least 12 to the small blind's 4. The previous raise increased the wager by 6, from 4 to 10; it did not increase it by 10.

    This is one legal line. Other legal choices are possible, and none is graded as a good strategy.

    Rule sources and limits

    Optional further study after the six stages

    The five tasks below are a menu for later study. They are not another beginner course to finish, and the external course is optional.

    Work at your own pace. A session can be split across several days, repeated, or skipped when you can already do its task. Use a deck on a table, a fictional example or a completed hand. None of these activities requires a wager.

    Keep two headings in your notes: “What I can now explain” and “What I still need to check.” Those notes are more informative than the number of pages opened. The linked external pages are free to read as listed, although their publishers may also sell products or advertise gambling.

    1. Tell the story of one hand.

    Read one hand from deal to showdown. Then close the page and describe the order: private cards, preflop betting, flop, turn, river and showdown if more than one player remains. Name who still has a decision at each step.

    Use the official hold'em rules and hand-rankings references below when you get stuck. Your output is a short explanation of a single hand, not a memorized glossary. Before moving on, explain why a hand can finish without anyone showing cards and why winning a pot does not equal gaining that whole amount in profit.

    2. Reconstruct a small pot.

    Use bets, calls and side pots, then write the separate contributions in a fictional heads-up river example. There are 60 chips in the pot before an opponent bets 30. Calling costs another 30, making the final pot 120. With no further betting or fees and ordinary showdown equity, the break-even share is 30 / 120 = 25%.

    Your task is to label the 60, the opponent's 30 and your additional 30. Do not divide by 90 simply because that is what you can see before calling. The free expected-value article below offers a second explanation. For a longer worked exercise, use the pot-odds workshop.

    3. Explain a decision before seeing the ending.

    Open the river Decision Lab. Before opening the answer panels, write the cost of calling and the assumption about the opponent that would matter most. Then inspect the two endings. Your output is one explanation that distinguishes the decision from its result.

    You do not have to guess the best action. Finding the missing information is useful. “The opponent could have a bluff” is a possibility, not a measurement of how frequently that opponent bluffs.

    4. Choose the kind of poker you want to understand.

    For live tournaments, use the field guide and identify three event details to confirm. For cash games, read the cash-game study guide and name the relevant costs. For Omaha or a mixed-game broadcast, use the game comparison before judging a showdown.

    Your output is a statement of the game, betting structure and question. An introductory hold'em rule is not a universal instruction for every game with poker chips.

    5. Study one lesson, not an entire archive.

    MIT's 2016 course page below provides a free university course with video lectures. It is historical teaching material, not a current commercial solver manual. Choose one lesson relevant to your question and note the assumptions behind its examples. The site listing does not mean every video has been watched or every claim independently reproduced.

    Finish with three sentences: the question, what the lesson helped clarify, and what it did not establish. Keep the next step small using the resource-check sheet. When the lesson is too advanced, return to the specific missing concept instead of concluding you need a more expensive course.

    A useful checkpoint

    You calculated a 25% break-even call. Have you shown that calling is correct?

    No. You have priced the call under stated conditions. You still need the hand's equity against an appropriate range and, when relevant, later actions, fees or tournament prize effects. The price and the evidence for meeting it are separate.

    Four free starting sources

    These are complementary starting points, not a ranking. Current listing descriptions, access and review limits come from the same catalogue as the full directory.
